title: No More Festivals: Exile Is Coming
summary: In the middle of a harvest celebration, Hosea tells Israel not to rejoice: they have been unfaithful to God on every threshing floor, and they will not stay in the LORD's land but go to Egypt and Assyria, where their festivals will cease. The prophet is mocked as a fool, but the days of punishment have come. God recalls how he found Israel like grapes in the wilderness, and how they gave themselves to Baal at Peor; now their glory will fly away, their children will be lost, and they will wander among the nations.
story: Chapter 8 announced that Israel would return to Egypt. Chapter 9 fills in what that exile will mean: no more feasts, no more offerings acceptable to God, no more children to carry the nation forward. The chapter also looks back, tracing Israel's unfaithfulness to its beginnings, to Baal-peor in the wilderness and to Gibeah in the days of the judges. The present crisis is not a sudden fall but the outworking of a long history. Chapter 10 will continue in the same vein, with more images from the vineyard and the field.
historical:
The setting of verses 1-9 seems to be a harvest festival, most likely the Feast of Tabernacles (Booths) in the autumn, when grain had been threshed and grapes pressed and the people celebrated with great joy (Deuteronomy 16:13-15). Many scholars think Hosea spoke these words publicly at such a festival, perhaps at Bethel, which would explain the hostile reaction in verses 7-8. The date is uncertain, but the threat of exile to Assyria and flight to Egypt fits the 730s or 720s BC, after Tiglath-pileser III had already deported people from Galilee and Gilead (2 Kings 15:29). Memphis, near modern Cairo, was one of Egypt's great cities and a vast burial ground, which gives force to the line Memphis will bury them. Some Israelites may well have fled to Egypt when Assyria struck, as Judeans later did after Babylon took Jerusalem (Jeremiah 43).

Hosea points to two episodes from the past. The days of Gibeah (verse 9) recall the outrage at Gibeah in Benjamin, where a Levite's concubine was abused and killed, leading to civil war (Judges 19 to 21); some scholars think Hosea may also have in mind Saul's kingship, which was based at Gibeah. Baal-peor (verse 10) refers to the incident in the wilderness when Israelite men joined in the worship of Baal of Peor with Moabite women, and a plague followed (Numbers 25). Gilgal (verse 15), where Saul was made king (1 Samuel 11:15), had become a center of corrupt worship.
cultural:
Threshing floors were flat, open areas where harvested grain was beaten and winnowed. They were places of celebration at harvest time and apparently also places of fertility rites linked with Baal, which is why Hosea speaks of love for hire on every threshing floor. In the ancient world a good harvest was often seen as payment from the gods, and Hosea turns that idea into an accusation.

In exile Israel would eat unclean food (verse 3). Outside the land, away from the altar, there was no way to offer firstfruits to God, and food could not be sanctified in the usual way. The bread of mourners (verse 4) was food in a house where someone had died; contact with the dead made everyone there ritually unclean (Numbers 19:14). The prophet as watchman (verse 8) was a familiar role: a lookout posted on a city wall to warn of danger (Ezekiel 3:17). And in a culture where children were the future of the family and the nation's strength, the loss of children (verses 11-16) was the most devastating image of judgment Hosea could use.
literary: The chapter falls into two parts. Verses 1-9 are a prophetic speech set against the festival, full of reversals: joy becomes mourning, the LORD's land becomes Assyria, the house of the LORD becomes a place of hostility. In verse 7 Hosea quotes the insults thrown at him, the prophet is a fool and the inspired man is insane, turning them back on his hearers. Verses 10-17 begin a new section in which God himself looks back on Israel's history, starting with a tender memory: grapes found in the wilderness, the first figs of the season, both rare delights. The contrast between that first delight and present rejection gives the chapter its grief. Wordplay runs throughout: Ephraim, whose name suggests fruitfulness, will bear no fruit (verse 16). The last verse is spoken by the prophet himself, a solemn verdict.

outline.t: Do not rejoice: festivals end in exile
The days of punishment; the prophet mocked
Grapes in the wilderness, shame at Baal-peor
Wickedness at Gilgal; wanderers among the nations

doctrines.note: At Baal-peor Israel consecrated themselves to Shame and became as detestable as the thing they loved (verse 10). People become like what they worship; idolatry reshapes the worshiper.
Exile takes away the festivals, offerings, and children that Israel treated as signs of blessing. Judgment removes the gifts that were enjoyed apart from the giver.

The prophet is called a fool and a madman (verse 7). God's messengers are often rejected precisely because their word exposes sin, and hostility to the prophet is a sign of how deep the sickness runs.
Remaining in the LORD's land depended on covenant faithfulness (Deuteronomy 28:63-64). They will not remain in the land of the LORD (verse 3); the land is his, and Israel held it as tenants.

words.note: Baal-peor, Baal of Peor, the god worshiped at Peor in Moab. The name stands for Israel's first great act of idolatry and sexual sin on the edge of the promised land (Numbers 25). Hosea treats it as the pattern of Israel's whole history: from the beginning, the people were drawn to Baal.

Boshet, shame. Consecrated themselves to Shame is a deliberate substitution: Israelite writers sometimes replaced the name Baal with boshet (compare names like Ish-bosheth, 2 Samuel 2:8, apparently originally Eshbaal, 1 Chronicles 8:33). The god they served is called what he brought them.

Tsaphah, to watch or keep lookout. The prophet is Ephraim's watchman, placed by God to warn the nation. Yet snares are set on his paths. The image shows both the prophet's responsibility and the people's hostility.

Nadad, to wander, flee, or be driven away. The chapter ends with Israel as wanderers among the nations (verse 17), echoing Cain, who became a wanderer after his sin (Genesis 4:12, where a similar-sounding word is used). The people God settled in a land will become homeless.

christ: The chapter's image of God finding Israel like grapes in the wilderness, a delight, belongs to the Bible's picture of Israel as God's vine or vineyard (Isaiah 5:1-7; Psalm 80:8-16). Jesus took up that picture when he called himself the true vine (John 15:1), the one in whom God's people finally bear fruit, where Ephraim was withered and could not bear fruit (verse 16). Hosea's experience as a watchman called a fool also anticipates the rejection of Jesus, whom some called out of his mind (Mark 3:21). And the promise that Israel's festivals would cease in exile is answered in the New Testament's picture of Jesus as the fulfillment of Israel's feasts (John 7:37-38, at the Feast of Tabernacles). These are connections of theme and pattern rather than direct predictions.

hard.q: How should we read the prayers for miscarriage and the slaying of children in verses 14-16?
hard.a:
These verses are among the most painful in the prophets. In verse 14 the prophet prays that God will give Israel wombs that miscarry and breasts that dry up, and in verse 16 God says he will slay the darlings of their wombs. Readers rightly recoil. Several considerations help. First, the verses speak of a nation, not of individual mothers: Ephraim's name suggests fruitfulness, and the judgment is the reversal of what Israel sought from Baal, fertility of womb and field. Having sought children from a fertility god, the nation will lose its future. Second, the prayer in verse 14 appears to begin as intercession (Give them, O LORD) and to break off in anguish (what will You give?), and many interpreters read Hosea as choosing, in a terrible situation, childlessness over the slaughter of children he foresaw in war (verse 13; compare 13:16). Third, the words describe what invasion and siege would bring, as history confirmed.

None of this makes the passage easy, and it should not be used to explain any particular family's loss as God's punishment. Jesus explicitly rejected that kind of reasoning about suffering (John 9:1-3; Luke 13:1-5). The prophets speak of national judgment under the covenant; they do not give readers license to read individual tragedies as verdicts.

questions: Israel celebrated its harvest while forgetting who gave it. How might our celebrations of good things drift away from gratitude to God?
The prophet was called a fool and a madman for speaking the truth. When have you found it hard to hear an uncomfortable word from God?
Israel became as detestable as the thing they loved. How have you seen people, including yourself, become like what they give themselves to?
